201.explanation: Among the thirty-five qualities Hemacandra's Yogaśāstra lists for the ideal Jain householder is being afraid of sin; Sangave notes that one who keeps these rules becomes, among other things, 'afraid of sinning.'
201.tie_back: Valluvar makes dread of evil the mark of the noble, and the Jain ideal householder is defined in the same way, by his apprehension of sin.
201.source: Hemacandra, Yogaśāstra, list of thirty-five qualities of the ideal householder, item 3, as rendered in Vilas A. Sangave, Jaina Ethics (jainworld.com)
201._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com (Sangave's English rendering of Hemacandra's list, not a full translation of the Yogaśāstra); a close match on fear of sin as a mark of the good, without the Kural's contrast with the hardened wicked.

202.quote_or_event: “Even such a thing as ghee when approached by the flame of fire will cause intolerable pain by fierce burning; of many bad actions will they become guilty who, though not crooked, become so, and associate with those who are bad.”
202.explanation: In its chapter titled 'The fear of misconduct', the Tamil Jain Nālaṭiyār uses the image of fire to warn that one wrong step, here keeping bad company, draws a person into many more bad actions.
202.tie_back: Valluvar says evil should be feared more than fire because it breeds more evil; the Nālaṭiyār also pairs fire with the way wrongdoing multiplies.
202.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 13 ('The fear of misconduct'), st. 4 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
202._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture. It is only a partial fit: the stanza is about bad company, and fire is a simile, not a measure of how much evil should be feared.

203.quote_or_event: “A monk should not be angry if beaten, nor should he therefore entertain sinful thoughts; knowing patience to be the highest good, a monk should meditate on the Law. If somebody strikes a restrained, resigned Śramaṇa somewhere, he should think: ‘I have not lost my life.’”
203.explanation: Mahāvīra's teaching on the 'troubles' (parīṣaha) a monk must bear includes being beaten. He must not answer with anger, or even with sinful thoughts, toward the one who strikes him.
203.tie_back: Valluvar calls refusing to harm even those who harm us the highest wisdom; the Jain canon likewise calls patience under attack 'the highest good' and forbids returning evil even in thought.
203._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi; diacritics normalized). A strong fit on not retaliating, though it is framed as monastic endurance, not the intellectual 'head of all knowledge' claim.

204.quote_or_event: “As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to kill. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to tyrannise over. As it would be unto thee, so it is with him whom thou intendest to torment… The righteous man who lives up to these sentiments, does therefore neither kill nor cause others to kill (living beings). He should not intentionally cause the same punishment for himself.”
204.explanation: The Ācārāṅga tells the would-be harmer that his intended victim is like himself. Jacobi's note explains that the pain one causes others in this life one will suffer in the next.
204.tie_back: Valluvar warns that whoever plots another's ruin brings ruin on himself; the Ācārāṅga addresses the person who 'intends' harm and says the punishment comes back to the plotter.
204.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.5.5.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
204._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi's translation; ellipsis marks an omitted sentence). It matches on intent and return, but in Jainism the return is impersonal karma, not Valluvar's personified Aram plotting back.

205.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.”
205.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana warns that wealth gained through evil deeds does not last: the one who gains it loses it and is trapped by his own passions.
205.tie_back: Valluvar refuses poverty as an excuse for evil because the evil-doer only ends up poorer; the Jain text likewise says wealth won by evil is lost.
205._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit on evil gain ending in loss, though it does not address need as a motive the way the Kural does.

206.quote_or_event: “All beings hate pains; therefore one should not kill them. This is the quintessence of wisdom: not to kill anything. Know this to be the legitimate conclusion from the principle of the reciprocity with regard to non-killing.”
206.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga bases ahiṃsā on reciprocity: every being shrinks from pain as one does oneself, and the same lecture tells the monk to treat all creatures 'so as he himself would be treated'.
206.tie_back: Valluvar tells whoever does not want suffering to stop inflicting it on others; the Jain reciprocity principle reasons the same way, from one's own hatred of pain to harming no one.
206.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.11.9–10, cf. I.11.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895)
206._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a close match on reciprocity, though the Jain text argues from empathy for others' pain more than from the karmic return the Kural stresses.

207.quote_or_event: “As the burglar caught in the breach of the wall perishes by the work the sinner himself had executed, thus people in this life and the next cannot escape the effect of their own actions.”
207.explanation: The burglar is crushed in the very hole he dug. In the same way, the Uttarādhyayana says no one escapes the results of his own deeds, in this life or the next.
207.tie_back: Valluvar says other enmities can be survived but the enmity of one's own evil deeds never dies; the Jain verse makes the same point with a man destroyed by his own handiwork.
207._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near match on inescapable karma across lives, without the Kural's explicit contrast with ordinary enmity.

208.quote_or_event: “As a young calf when let loose among a number of cows naturally seeks out and attaches itself to its own mother, so does the act of a former state of existence seek out and attach itself to him who has performed it.”
208.explanation: The Jain Nālaṭiyār pictures past karma as a calf that unerringly finds its own mother in a herd: a deed finds and clings to the one who did it.
208.tie_back: Valluvar's shadow that never leaves the evil-doer's feet and the Nālaṭiyār's calf that seeks out its mother are both images of a deed's result that cannot be separated from its doer.
208.source: Nālaṭiyār, ch. 11 ('The effect of actions done in a former birth'), st. 1 (English translation in The Indian Antiquary, via wisdomlib.org)
208._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; this is a Tamil Jain text, used because its image of karma clinging to its doer is the closest parallel to the Kural's shadow simile.

209.quote_or_event: “Man! Thou art thy own friend; why wishest thou for a friend beyond thyself? … Man! restraining thyself (from the outward world) ‘thou wilt get free from pain.’”
209.explanation: The Ācārāṅga tells each person that he is his own friend, and that restraint, not outside help, frees one from pain.
209.tie_back: Valluvar says anyone who truly loves himself will keep away from every evil; the Ācārāṅga likewise makes the self its own friend, and self-restraint the way to escape suffering.
209.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.3.3.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
209._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (Jacobi's translation; ellipsis marks omitted text). A strong thematic fit on rightly understood self-interest, though it does not mention avoiding even the slightest evil.

210.quote_or_event: “A careful man who does not injure living beings, is called ‘circumspect’ (samita). The sinful Karman will quit him as water quits raised ground. In thoughts, words, and acts he should do nothing injurious to beings who people the world, whether they move or not.”
210.explanation: Kapila's verses promise that sinful karma runs off the careful, harmless person as water runs off high ground, provided he does no harm in thought, word or deed.
210.tie_back: Valluvar assures the one who never strays from the right path into evil that he is safe from ruin; the Jain text says sinful karma cannot settle on such a person.
210._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit on the person who avoids evil being protected, though stated in terms of karma and non-injury, not 'ruin'.
